title: Light induced superconducting diode effect in patterned films
authors: Evan M. Wilson, Hou-Tong Chen, Alexander V. Balatsky
abstract: Structured light offers a route to control superconducting transport without permanently modifying the material or applying a static bias. Here we show that structured optical driving can generate a superconducting diode response in patterned superconducting films with asymmetric holes. Using generalized time-dependent Ginzburg Landau simulations, we find that optical driving produces rectified dc photovoltages and zero bias directional supercurrent imbalance in a junction free geometry, with continuous-drive diode efficiencies of order $10^{-3}$ and pulsed efficiencies reaching $10^{-2}$. The response is controlled by both the hole array and the optical mode. Increasing the number of asymmetric holes enhances rectification, reversing circular helicity reverses the diode polarity, and the optical spatial mode strongly modifies the magnitude and polarity of the directional response. Pulsed excitation enhances the zero bias line cut current imbalance to the percent level. For linearly polarized illumination, the asymmetric metacrystal converts the drive into local chiral supercurrent motion, inducing an inverse Faraday effect like mechanism for dynamical time reversal symmetry breaking. These results establish patterned superconducting films as a viable platform for light-tunable superconducting diode behavior.
summary: The research shows that patterned superconducting films act as superconducting diodes when illuminated by structured light. By exploiting the geometric asymmetry of holes (metacrystals), the system generates a directional supercurrent imbalance and measurable photovoltage even without external bias. This establishes a powerful, non-invasive method for controlling superconducting transport using optical fields.
main_problem: The study demonstrates how structured light can induce a superconducting diode response in patterned films without applying a static bias or permanently altering the material.
main_result: Structured optical driving generates measurable, non-zero directional supercurrent imbalances and rectified photovoltages, establishing patterned superconductors as viable platforms for light-tunable diodes.
method: The analysis relies on solving the generalized time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau equation using numerical simulations to model the coherent condensate response.
model_or_system: The physical system is a superconducting film perforated with geometrically asymmetric holes (metacrystals). The dynamics are governed by the TDGL equation, incorporating an optical drive via a time-dependent vector potential.
key_observables: Rectified dc photovoltages ($V_{dc}$), zero-bias directional supercurrent imbalance ($\eta_{LR}, \eta_{UD}$), and the nonlinear dependence of $V_{dc}$ on optical intensity.
important_parameters: The response is highly controlled by the hole array geometry, the helicity ($s$), and orbital angular momentum index ($\ell$) of the incident structured light.
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses exclusively on the coherent condensate response, neglecting dissipative effects like optical heating or nonequilibrium quasiparticle dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup using structured light, show time-dependent current textures revealing chiral flow patterns, and plot $V_{dc}$ vs. intensity to confirm nonlinear rectification.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes how structural asymmetry interacts with various optical modes (Gaussian, Laguerre-Gaussian) under both continuous and pulsed driving conditions to quantify the resulting directional supercurrent imbalance and photovoltage.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum electrodynamics/optics with superconductivity, showing how engineered geometry can induce non-linear, directed transport phenomena using light, which is relevant for understanding coherent control in mesoscopic superconducting circuits.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A superconducting film patterned with an Nx × Ny array of asymmetric holes is illuminated by a structured optical beam. The drive is described by a vector potential A(s,ℓ,p)(r, t), where s denotes helicity, ℓthe orbital angular momentum index, and p the radial index. The induced condensate dynamics are modeled using the time-dependent Ginzburg–Landau equation, with the supercurrent density js determined by the gauge-covariant phase gradients of the superconducting order parameter.

FIG. 2. Optically induced sheet-current texture in the 169-hole superconducting metacrystal for the continuous linearly polarized Gaussian drive, (s, ℓ, p) = (0, 0, 0). The color scale shows the magnitude of the induced current, and the horizontal and vertical central cuts mark the internal channels used to compare left-right and up-down current flow. The asymmetric hole array redirects the driven current into components parallel and perpendicular to the driving electric field, enabling a zero-bias directional current imbalance. Video simulations for all optical modes are available on the companion website [32].

FIG. 3. Time-dependent zero-bias current imbalance and local phase mixing in the 169-hole superconducting metacrystal under continuous linearly polarized Gaussian illumination, (s, ℓ, p) = (0, 0, 0). Panel (a) shows the instantaneous left–right and up–down diode-like coefficients, ηLR and ηUD, obtained from opposite central line-cut currents. The instantaneous coefficients are plotted as dimensionless ratios, so η = 0.10 corresponds to 10%; Table I reports the cycle-averaged values in percent. The asymmetric peaks over an optical cycle produce a finite cycle-averaged directional imbalance. Panel (b) shows representative local current components Jx(t) and Jy(t) inside the patterned region....

FIG. 4. (a) For Gaussian linear polarization, (s, ℓ, p) = (0, 0, 0), the dc voltage shows nonlinear rectification as a function of the optical intensity proxy E2 0. The response includes a sign change at low intensity and higher-order nonlinearity. (b) Circularly polarized beams with opposite optical helicities, (s, ℓ, p) = (+1, 0, 0) and (−1, 0, 0), separate into opposite-sign voltage branches that both change sign, showing helicity-sensitive rectification.

FIG. 5. Geometry dependence and harmonic content of the optically rectified voltage for the linearly polarized Gaussian drive, (s, ℓ, p) = (0, 0, 0). Panel (a) shows the dc voltage as the number of asymmetric holes is increased for the original hole orientation and for the 180◦-rotated geometry. The voltage grows with hole number and approaches a metacrystal plateau, while rotating the holes reverses the sign of the response, showing that the diode polarity is set by the broken spatial symmetry of the hole array.
